lesson.title: Fear of Red: America's First Red Scare
lesson.summary: In 1919 and 1920, fears of communist revolution, fueled by labor unrest and a wave of anarchist bombings, triggered a nationwide panic that swept up radicals, immigrants, and ordinary union members alike.
lesson.body:
The machinery of wartime suppression did not shut off when World War I ended. During the war, Congress had passed the Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918, laws that made it a crime to interfere with the draft or to criticize the government, the flag, or the military. Federal courts upheld these laws, most notably in the 1919 Supreme Court case Schenck v. United States, where Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. ruled that speech creating a clear and present danger was not protected. That legal and political apparatus for punishing dissent was still fully in place when a new fear replaced fear of Germany: fear of Bolshevism.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 had brought the world's first communist state to power, and Vladimir Lenin's Bolsheviks made no secret of their hope that revolution would spread. American radicals, from anarchists to socialists to newly formed communist parties, seemed to confirm the danger was real. The postwar economy made things worse. Inflation was high, veterans were returning to a tight job market, and workers who had held off on strikes during the war now pushed hard for better wages and conditions. More than four million American workers went on strike in 1919 alone. The Seattle General Strike in February shut down an entire city. The Boston police force walked off the job in September, leaving the city temporarily without law enforcement. A massive steel strike spread across the industrial Midwest. To many middle class Americans, these strikes looked less like ordinary labor disputes and more like the opening moves of a revolution.

Then came the bombs. On June 2, 1919, coordinated bombings struck eight cities, including one at the Washington home of Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, planted by an Italian anarchist who died in the blast. The bombings, combined with the strikes and the specter of Bolshevism, convinced many Americans that a violent radical uprising was imminent. Newspapers ran lurid headlines about the Red menace. State legislatures passed criminal syndicalism laws targeting radical political organizing. Immigrants, especially those from Southern and Eastern Europe, became particular targets of suspicion, since many prominent anarchists and socialists were foreign born. This climate of fear, building directly on the wartime precedent that dissent could be treated as a crime, set the stage for the government's own crackdown, the Palmer Raids.
